title: Lena and the Semester
premise: Kestrel Almeida, the varsity team's statistician, has spent two years quietly proving to herself that the school's championship seasons are built on doctored eligibility records — and burying the proof, because exposing it would destroy the scholarship futures of the players she loves. When her college application essay accidentally answers an honesty prompt with a fragment of the truth, a counselor reads it, and suddenly Kestrel is the only person standing between the school board's cover-up and a deadline that will seal both her admission and the records' destruction. As she races to gather testimony from teammates who'd rather stay silent, she discovers the original scandal involved a player who died years ago and was erased from every roster. In the end, Kestrel publishes everything at the cost of her own acceptance letter, choosing truth over survival — and finds that the community she feared losing is the one that finally sees her.
about_author: Sebastian Crane is the pen name of a former high-school debate coach who spent a decade watching teenagers learn what silence costs. He writes young adult fiction about the moment loyalty and truth stop being friends.

chapters.title: The Numbers Don't Lie
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. During a championship game she tracks stats from the bleachers, mentally reconciling them against eligibility files she knows were altered. Her best friend Dev scores the winning basket on an ineligible transcript. The beat: comfortable complicity, the thrill of belonging outweighing the itch of guilt.

chapters.title: One Honest Question
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. In study hall she opens the college essay prompt: 'Describe a truth you kept, and what it cost.' She writes three reckless sentences about rigged rosters before deleting them — but autosave submits a draft to the shared counseling portal. Beat: dread arriving in real time.

chapters.title: Ms. Okafor Reads Everything
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. The college counselor calls her in, not angry but attentive, and asks whether the deleted draft was fiction. Kestrel lies badly. Ms. Okafor mentions, offhand, a boy named Marcus Vale who played for Kestrel's team six years ago. Beat: the first crack in the wall.

chapters.title: Who Was Marcus Vale?
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, intercut with found documents. Yearbooks show Marcus on the 2018 roster; current archives show nothing. A librarian lets slip that his records were purged after he died in a car crash the night before a playoff game. Beat: grief for a stranger, and suspicion hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: Dev Makes Her Promise
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. He senses Kestrel pulling away and extracts a promise: whatever she's doing, don't blow up their season before signing day. His own mother's job depends on his scholarship. Beat: love weaponized as a leash.

chapters.title: The Board's Quiet Meeting
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She tails the school board to a closed session and hears them vote to digitize-and-shred old athletic files by month's end. A board member, Ruth Calloway, catches her in the hallway and says only: 'You have until then.' Beat: a ticking clock handed over like a dare.

chapters.title: Testimony of the Second String
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Kestrel interviews benched players who suspected the fraud but stayed quiet for playing time. One, Priya, agrees to go on record; another threatens to report Kestrel instead. Beat: solidarity is not automatic — it has to be bought with risk.

chapters.title: Coach Reyes Knows
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She confronts Coach Reyes, who admits he inherited the falsified system and kept it running because refusing meant losing every kid to colleges that recruit off winning records. He begs her to think about who gets hurt. Beat: the antagonist becomes almost sympathetic, which is worse.

chapters.title: Marcus's Mother
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. She tracks down Denise Vale, who has spent six years asking why her son's academic record vanished the week after his death. Denise gives Kestrel a box of Marcus's transcripts — real ones. Beat: the abstract scandal acquires a face and a funeral.

chapters.title: What the Essay Started
chapters.summary: Ms. Okafor's POV. Under pressure from the principal, she must report the draft or protect the student. She stalls, digging into Marcus's file herself, and finds a memo signed by the current board chair. Beat: an adult chooses the kid over the institution.

chapters.title: Signing Day
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev signs his letter of intent in front of cameras while Kestrel watches, holding evidence that could void it. He catches her eye afterward and knows. That night he asks her directly if she's going to ruin him. Beat: the friendship reaches its breaking point.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Ruth Calloway offers Kestrel a deal: full scholarship endorsement and sealed records, in exchange for her silence and her essay file. Kestrel realizes they're scared enough to bargain. Beat: temptation dressed as mercy.

chapters.title: Priya Recants
chapters.summary: Priya's POV. After her family receives a vague threat about her visa status, Priya withdraws her statement. Kestrel rages, then understands — everyone's survival has a price, and she's been counting other people's money. Beat: guilt inverted; the statistician learns some losses aren't betrayal.

chapters.title: The Backup Nobody Deleted
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Following Marcus's transcripts, she finds the district's old backup server still holds the original eligibility audits — including one flagging Marcus as falsely declared ineligible weeks before his death. Beat: the cover-up wasn't hiding cheating; it was hiding a death they caused.

chapters.title: Everything Is Fine
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. A false-calm chapter: Kestrel goes through the motions of senior life, nearly convinces herself to take the deal, and drafts an acceptance of Calloway's offer. Then she rereads Marcus's mother's letters. Beat: the quiet before the choice.

chapters.title: Dev Chooses
chapters.summary: Dev's POV. Dev finds the backup files himself and reads what was done to Marcus — a player exactly like him. He brings the drive to Kestrel and tells her to burn it all down, even if his name burns too. Beat: loyalty finally aligned with truth.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. With shredding scheduled for morning, the group — Kestrel, Dev, Ms. Okafor, Denise Vale — works overnight to copy, verify, and package the records for the press and the state athletics board. Beat: frantic, hopeful momentum; the team she never captained finally huddles.

chapters.title: The Shredding Room
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Kestrel confronts Calloway and Coach Reyes in the records room as the truck arrives, buying time by reading Marcus's name aloud into the record. Reyes, broken, hands over his own copies. Beat: climax of nerve — one girl's voice against an institution's machinery.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. The story breaks: headlines, emergency board session, players pulled from playoffs, scholarships suspended pending review — including Dev's. Kestrel watches the fallout she chose. Beat: victory that feels like wreckage; the price comes due.

chapters.title: What It Cost
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Her early-admission offer is rescinded over the 'inappropriate essay.' Dev's scholarship is reinstated after state review clears the players. Denise Vale speaks at the board meeting, saying Marcus's name into the minutes. Beat: accounting — losses tallied honestly, no rounding down.

chapters.title: The Rewrite
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. Asked to resubmit her college essay, Kestrel writes the whole truth this time and signs it. Ms. Okafor mails it without edits. Beat: reclamation — the question that started everything finally answered in full.

chapters.title: Lena and the Semester
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, months later. At graduation, a plaque with Marcus Vale's name goes up in the gym. An acceptance letter arrives from a college whose admissions reader wrote back: 'We admitted you for the essay you told the truth in.' Beat: resolution — survival redefined as being seen.
